contains-duplicate.statement: Return true when any value appears more than once in the array.
contains-duplicate.invariant: Before each iteration, the set contains every earlier value. A failed insertion therefore proves that the current value equals an earlier one. If every insertion succeeds, all values are distinct.
contains-duplicate.complexity: Expected time O(n) and auxiliary space O(n). HashSet operations are expected O(1).
contains-duplicate.example: Example [2, 1, 3, 1]: value = 2 is added to seen, then 1 and 3 are added. On the next value, 1 is already present, so add(1) returns false and the method returns true.
contains-duplicate.tests:
Input
 | Expected

[1,2,3,1]
 | true

[1,2,3,4]
 | false

[]
 | false (no duplicate possible)
contains-duplicate.constraints:
Do not compare every pair; that is O(n squared).
A one-element or empty array has no duplicate.
Sorting can use less auxiliary space but changes the array and costs O(n log n).

valid-anagram.statement: Decide whether two strings contain exactly the same characters with the same multiplicities.
valid-anagram.invariant: Each slot records count in s minus count in t. All slots are zero exactly when every character occurs equally often in both strings.
valid-anagram.complexity: Time O(n) and auxiliary space O(1) for the fixed lowercase-English alphabet.
valid-anagram.example: Example s = "cat", t = "act": at i = 0, s.charAt(0) is 'c' and t.charAt(0) is 'a', so count['c' - 'a'] becomes 1 and count['a' - 'a'] becomes -1. At i = 1, 'a' adds 1 and 'c' subtracts 1, cancelling both slots; i = 2 does the same for 't'. Every slot ends at 0, so the strings are anagrams.
valid-anagram.tests:
Input
 | Expected

s="anagram", t="nagaram"
 | true

s="rat", t="car"
 | false

s="a", t="ab"
 | false (length mismatch)
valid-anagram.constraints:
Confirm the character set; use a HashMap for arbitrary Unicode code points.
Equal length alone is not enough.
Sorting works but costs O(n log n).

two-sum.statement: Return indices of two distinct elements whose values add to the target.
two-sum.invariant: When processing index i, the map contains exactly the earlier elements. Finding the complement gives a distinct earlier index whose sum with nums[i] is the target. The promised solution will eventually expose such a pair.
two-sum.complexity: Expected time O(n) and auxiliary space O(n).
two-sum.example: Example nums = [2, 7, 11, 15], target = 9: at i = 0, need = 9 - 2 = 7; 7 is not in the map, so store 2 -> 0. At i = 1, need = 9 - 7 = 2; the map contains 2 -> 0, so return [0, 1].

group-anagrams.statement: Group strings that are anagrams of one another.
group-anagrams.invariant: Two lowercase strings produce the same signature exactly when every letter count matches, which is the definition of being anagrams. The map therefore places precisely the anagrams together.
group-anagrams.complexity: Time O(total characters) and auxiliary space O(total characters) for the returned groups and keys.
group-anagrams.example: Example ["eat", "tea", "bat"]: for "eat", increment e, a, and t to build key [1,0,0,0,1,...,1]. "tea" creates the same key, so it joins the same list; "bat" creates a different key and starts another list.
group-anagrams.constraints:
A separator prevents ambiguous keys such as counts 1,11 and 11,1.
The empty string has an all-zero signature and groups correctly.
If the alphabet is not fixed, sort each string or use a map-based key.

top-k-frequent-elements.statement: Return the k values that occur most often.
top-k-frequent-elements.invariant: Every value is placed in the bucket equal to its exact frequency. Visiting buckets in descending order therefore encounters values from most frequent to least frequent, so the first k are a valid answer.
top-k-frequent-elements.complexity: Time O(n) and auxiliary space O(n).

product-of-array-except-self.statement: For every index, return the product of all other elements without division.
product-of-array-except-self.invariant: After the first pass, answer[i] equals the product strictly left of i. During the reverse pass, suffix equals the product strictly right of i. Their product therefore excludes exactly nums[i].
product-of-array-except-self.complexity: Time O(n). Auxiliary space O(1) excluding the required output array.
product-of-array-except-self.example: Example nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]: the prefix pass leaves result [1, 1, 2, 6]. The suffix pass starts with suffix = 1; at i = 3, result[3] = 6 * 1 = 6, then suffix becomes 4. At i = 2, result[2] = 2 * 4 = 8, and so on, producing [24, 12, 8, 6].
product-of-array-except-self.constraints:
Update the running product after assigning the current index.
Zeros work naturally; division does not.
The empty-product identity is 1 at an array boundary.

encode-and-decode-strings.invariant: The decoder first recovers the encoded length and then consumes exactly the original payload, regardless of characters inside it. Advancing to the next prefix reconstructs every item in order.
encode-and-decode-strings.complexity: Time O(total encoded characters) for both operations. The output and decoded list require O(total characters) space.
encode-and-decode-strings.example: Example ["hello", "world"]: encode hello as "5#hello" and world as "5#world". During decoding, read digits until '#', parse 5, then consume exactly the next five characters; the delimiter remains safe even if the text contains '#'.

Do not split on # because the payload may contain #.

longest-consecutive-sequence.statement: Find the length of the longest run of consecutive integer values in an unsorted array.
longest-consecutive-sequence.invariant: Every maximal consecutive sequence has one smallest value and only that value passes the start test. The inner walk counts the entire sequence once, so the maximum over starts is the desired length.
longest-consecutive-sequence.complexity: Expected time O(n) and auxiliary space O(n). Although nested, the walks collectively visit each distinct value once from a valid start.
longest-consecutive-sequence.example: Example [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2]: start only at 1 because 0 is absent. Check 1, 2, 3, 4 one by one, giving length 4; values 100 and 200 are also starts but produce length 1.
longest-consecutive-sequence.constraints:
Duplicates do not lengthen a sequence because the set removes them.
Starting a walk from every value degrades to O(n squared) on long runs.
Be aware of integer overflow if constraints allow Integer.MAX_VALUE.

valid-palindrome.statement: Determine whether the alphanumeric characters form a palindrome when case is ignored.
valid-palindrome.invariant: At every comparison, all meaningful characters outside the pointers have already matched. Skipping ignored characters preserves the normalized sequence. If the pointers cross without a mismatch, that sequence equals its reverse.
valid-palindrome.complexity: Time O(n) and auxiliary space O(1).
valid-palindrome.example: Example "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama": left and right move inward while skipping punctuation and spaces. At each comparison, lower-case both characters; every pair matches, so return true.

 | true

Move both pointers after a successful comparison.

3sum.statement: Return all unique triples whose values sum to zero.
3sum.invariant: For a fixed first value, pointer movement discards only pairs that cannot reach zero because of sorted order. Thus every feasible pair is considered. Duplicate skipping removes repeated value triples without removing any distinct triple.
3sum.complexity: Time O(n squared) and auxiliary space O(1) apart from sorting implementation and output.
3sum.example: Example [-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4]: after sorting to [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2], fix -1 at i = 1. Set left = 2 and right = 5; -1 + -1 + 2 = 0, so record [-1, -1, 2] and move past duplicates.
3sum.constraints:
Skip a repeated first value.
After a match, move both pointers and skip duplicates.
Use a wider numeric type if constraints can overflow a three-value sum.

container-with-most-water.statement: Choose two vertical lines that contain the largest area of water.
container-with-most-water.invariant: When the shorter side is discarded, no pair using it at a smaller width can exceed the current area. Therefore each discarded boundary cannot belong to an unseen better solution, and the maximum encountered is optimal.
container-with-most-water.complexity: Time O(n) and auxiliary space O(1).
container-with-most-water.example: Example heights [1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7]: at left = 0 and right = 8, area = min(1, 7) * 8 = 8. Move the shorter height, left, because moving the taller side cannot increase the limiting height; later the pair 8 and 7 gives area 49.
container-with-most-water.constraints:
The limiting height is the minimum, not the maximum.
Moving both pointers can skip the optimum.
Use long internally if width times height may overflow int.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock.invariant: The running minimum is the cheapest valid buy before or at the current position. The computed profit is therefore the best trade ending here, and the maximum over all endings is the best single trade.

longest-substring-without-repeating-char.statement: Find the longest contiguous substring containing no repeated character.
longest-substring-without-repeating-char.invariant: After adjusting left, the window contains no repeated current character, and earlier repetitions were already excluded. Taking the maximum length over every right endpoint considers the longest valid substring.
longest-substring-without-repeating-char.complexity: Time O(n) and auxiliary space O(min(n, alphabet size)).
longest-substring-without-repeating-char.example: Example "abcabcbb": right advances through a, b, c. At the next a, the window has a duplicate, so move left past the old a; the valid window becomes "bca" and the maximum length remains 3.
longest-substring-without-repeating-char.constraints:
Never move left backward when a previous occurrence lies outside the window.
Update the last index after using its old value.
Clarify whether Java char units or Unicode code points define a character.

longest-repeating-character-replacement.statement: Find the longest substring that can become one repeated character after at most k replacements.
longest-repeating-character-replacement.invariant: Any window satisfying size minus maxCount at most k can be converted by replacing all non-majority characters. The possibly stale maxCount can delay shrinking but cannot create a best length that was never feasible when that maximum was established.
longest-repeating-character-replacement.complexity: Time O(n) and auxiliary space O(1) for the fixed uppercase-English alphabet.
longest-repeating-character-replacement.example: For "AABABBA", k=1, window "AABA" has length 4 and maxCount=3, so best=4. Adding B makes length−maxCount=2; remove the left A. maxCount stays at its historical value 3 after shrinking: the new window need not itself be valid, but cannot increase best beyond an already achievable length. The final maximum is 4.

 | Expected

 | 4 (replace both A's or both B's)

"AABABBA", k=1
 | 4

"AAAA", k=2
 | 4 (no replacement needed)
longest-repeating-character-replacement.constraints:
The required replacements equal window length minus the majority count.
A stale maxCount is intentional in the standard linear solution.
Use a map when the alphabet is not fixed.

minimum-window-substring.statement: Return the shortest substring of s containing every character of t with required multiplicity.
minimum-window-substring.invariant: The expansion finds every point at which a valid window can end. The inner loop removes every unnecessary leading character, so it examines the minimum valid window for that endpoint. The best among them is globally minimum.
minimum-window-substring.complexity: Time O(|s| + |t|) and auxiliary space O(alphabet size). Each pointer moves only forward.
minimum-window-substring.example: Example s = "ADOBECODEBANC", t = "ABC": expand right until the window contains A, B, and C. Once valid, move left while counts still cover t; "BANC" is reduced to the minimum valid window "BANC".

Counts, not mere membership, matter when t repeats a character.

valid-parentheses.statement: Check whether every opening bracket is closed by the correct bracket in the correct order.
valid-parentheses.invariant: The stack represents closers required by still-open brackets, with the next required closer on top. Every processed closer must match it. An empty stack at the end means no unmatched opener remains.

binary-search.statement: Return an index of target in a nondecreasing sorted integer array, or -1 if absent.
binary-search.invariant: If target exists, a matching index remains in [low, high].
binary-search.complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space: each comparison halves the remaining interval.
binary-search.example: [1, 3, 5], target 5: midpoint 1 has value 3; low becomes 2; midpoint 2 matches; return 2.
binary-search.constraints: Non-null sorted int array; duplicate targets may return any matching index.

find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array.statement: Find the minimum value in a rotated strictly increasing array.
find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array.invariant: When nums[mid] exceeds nums[right], the sorted order breaks between mid and right, so the minimum is strictly right of mid. Otherwise the segment from mid to right is sorted and mid remains a possible minimum, so right can move to mid.
find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array.complexity: Time O(log n) and auxiliary space O(1).
find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array.example: Example [3, 4, 5, 1, 2]: left = 0, mid = 2, right = 4. Because nums[mid] = 5 is greater than nums[right] = 2, the minimum must be right of mid, so set left = mid + 1; the answer is 1.
find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array.constraints:
Use right equals mid, not mid minus one, when mid may be the minimum.
This logic assumes distinct values; duplicates require a modified rule.
An unrotated array still works.

reverse-linked-list.statement: Reverse a singly linked list and return its new head.
reverse-linked-list.invariant: Before each iteration, previous heads the correctly reversed processed prefix and current heads the untouched suffix. One pointer change moves current into the reversed prefix while preserving the suffix via next.
reverse-linked-list.complexity: Time O(n) and auxiliary space O(1).

merge-two-sorted-lists.statement: Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted list by reusing their nodes.
merge-two-sorted-lists.invariant: At each step, tail ends a sorted prefix containing the smallest consumed nodes. Choosing the smaller current head preserves sorted order. Once one list ends, the other remainder is already sorted and no smaller node remains elsewhere.

reorder-list.invariant: The split preserves the original order of the first half. Reversal exposes last nodes in the order required by the output. Weaving consumes exactly one node from each sequence, producing the requested alternation without losing nodes.
